title: Vocabulary and Context Clues

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Imagine a jigsaw puzzle with one piece missing. You do not need the box lid to know what belongs there, because the pieces touching the hole tell you it must be sky, or grass, or part of a wheel. An unfamiliar word is that missing piece, and the sentences around it are the connecting pieces. Reading them to work out the word's meaning is exactly what using context clues means.

### Question 2

If a friend says, "Unlike my loud brother, my sister is taciturn," you were never given a definition, but you were given a mirror. Loud stands on one side, so taciturn has to be the reflection: quiet. Words like unlike, however, and whereas are the frame around that mirror, warning you to look for the opposite instead of a match. That is a contrast, or antonym, clue.

### Question 3

Treat the commas as a pair of doors that swing open right after the hard word, with the answer stacked behind them. "Cyanosis" opens the doors, and out comes "a bluish discoloration of the skin." You never had to guess, because the writer restated the term in plain language on the spot. That built-in answer key is a definition or restatement clue, and it is the easiest kind to spot once you watch for the punctuation.

### Question 4

Guessing a word from thin context is like identifying an animal from one paw print. Sliding the print to a different spot in the mud, or pointing at it, adds nothing. What helps is more evidence right beside it: a tuft of fur, a tail drag, a stride length. An appositive is that extra evidence, a short plain-language explanation parked next to the word so the reader does not have to reconstruct it alone.

### Question 5

Signal words are road signs telling you which way to steer. "Or" and "in other words" are a straight-ahead sign: the next idea points the same direction, so copy it over. "However" and "unlike" are a U-turn sign: the next idea points the other way, so flip it before you keep it. The clue-reading skill is identical in both cases; only the steering changes, and the sign tells you which.

### Question 6

This one is detective work rather than reading an answer key. Nobody defines sluggish, but you are shown two shifts back to back, slowed movement, and the same chart line read three times. Assemble those details and the picture is unmistakable: slow and heavy, like wading through deep mud. Because you built the meaning from the whole scene rather than from a stated definition, this is a general-sense, or inference, clue.

### Question 7

A cause-and-effect clue is a domino chain you can read from either end. You are handed the first domino, dehydration, and the last one, skin that stays pinched up instead of snapping back. The unknown word sits in the middle of that chain, so it has to name the springiness that failed. Connectors like because, so, and as a result are the tip-off that a chain is there to follow.

### Question 8

Picture a stale cracker next to a strip of leather. The sentence tells you this tissue rips when barely touched, which is cracker behavior, not leather behavior, so friable has to mean crumbly and easily torn. The transferable move is to let the second half of the sentence, the part reporting what actually happened, define the mystery word in the first half.

### Question 9

When you infer a meaning, name the evidence you used. Here two pieces do the work: "unlike" is a U-turn sign telling you the condition is the opposite of sudden, and the ending spells that out, since months passed before anyone noticed. Think of a slow roof leak that soaks a ceiling all season before the stain appears. Checking that both pieces really say what you think is how you catch a guess built on nothing but a word's ominous sound.

### Question 10

Some words are like a key that opens more than one lock, and the sentence tells you which door you are standing at. "Culture" can mean a group's traditions or a taste for the arts, but here the door is labeled wound and antibiotics. At that door, culture means growing a sample in the lab to find out which organism is present. The rule is simple: let the neighboring words choose the meaning for you.

### Question 11

Context clues are like guessing someone's job from their scrubs and badge. You can tell they work in the hospital, which is genuinely useful, but you may not know whether they are a respiratory therapist or a phlebotomist. For general reading, the category is enough; when the exact term will appear in your own charting or on an exam, you still have to confirm it. Treat the inference as a solid first draft, not the final answer.

### Question 12

Two clues converge on one answer here. The front of the word, hem-, is a name tag reading blood, the same tag you see on hemoglobin and hematoma. The sentence then tells you where that blood came from: a coughing fit, with red streaks in the basin. Put the name tag beside the scene and you get coughing up blood. Word parts tell you the family a term belongs to; context tells you which member of the family is on the page.
